title: Periodontal treatment
blurb: BPE codes and what they mean for treatment, scaling and root surface debridement, the instruments, review and lifelong maintenance.
question: A patient who hasn't attended for three years has heavy calculus, bleeding gums and a BPE with a code 4 in one sextant. The hygienist plans treatment with the ultrasonic scaler. What comes first, what do you set up and check, and how will everyone know whether treatment has worked?

teach.body: Periodontal disease is driven by plaque bacteria at the gum margin. Gingivitis (inflamed, bleeding gums) is reversible. Periodontitis has destroyed some of the tooth's attachment and bone, forming pockets, and the lost support doesn't grow back. Treatment aims to remove the plaque and calculus, help the patient control plaque at home, reduce risk factors such as smoking and poorly controlled diabetes, and keep the disease stable for life. Dentists, hygienists and therapists carry it out; you support every stage.

teach.caption: Bone has been lost and a true pocket has formed, with calculus on the root surface below the gum where a toothbrush can't reach.
BPE (BSP 2019): WHO probe with a 0.5 mm ball and a black band at 3.5–5.5 mm. The highest code in each sextant is recorded; * is added to the number, e.g. 3*.

head: Code
Management
rows: OHI, plus remove calculus and plaque traps such as overhangs
As 2, plus root surface debridement; chart that sextant after treatment
Full-mouth pocket chart before and after treatment; consider referral

steps.label: Step 1: foundations
steps.sub: OHI, risk factors, remove visible deposits

steps.label: Step 2: below the gum
steps.sub: Root surface debridement, often under LA

teach.caption: Re-evaluation compares the new pocket chart with the first. Sites that don't respond may need more instrumentation, surgery or referral to a specialist.
Afterwards, teeth feel smoother because the rough deposits have gone.

1: tray with the ultrasonic scaler handpiece. 2: hand instruments (probes and scalers). 3: ultrasonic scaler handpiece and tip. 4: magnifying loupes. 6: an instrument working at the gum margin of an inflamed tooth.

teach.body: The ultrasonic tip vibrates very fast and gets hot, so it needs a water coolant: check the water flow before the session starts. The water and vibration create a heavy aerosol, so the high-volume aspirator must sit close to the working site; a misty view means reposition the suction. Give the patient safety glasses. If the patient feels sharp sensitivity, pause and reassess their comfort; local anaesthetic may be offered for deep work.

teach.h: Is it working? Review and maintenance
teach.body: At review, the pocket chart is repeated and compared with the first one. Success looks like less bleeding on probing and shallower pockets. If plaque persists, the answer is to reinforce oral hygiene, because no amount of scaling can make up for daily cleaning. As inflammation settles, gums may shrink back, so teeth can look longer and feel sensitive. Over-instrumentation can lacerate the gum. Long term, patients need regular supportive periodontal care.

teach.text: The first priority is NOT surgery or referral: it is oral hygiene instruction and removing deposits. And at review, the key sign of success is LESS BLEEDING ON PROBING, not whiter or shinier teeth.

items: BPE: 0 healthy, 1 bleeding, 2 calculus or overhang, 3 pocket 3.5–5.5 mm, 4 over 5.5 mm, * furcation.
Step 1 OHI and deposit removal; Step 2 root surface debridement; Step 3 re-evaluate and treat non-responding sites; Step 4 maintain.
Graduated probe for pockets; ultrasonic (check water first, HVA close); curettes for subgingival deposits.
Success = less bleeding on probing and shallower pockets. Plaque persists = reinforce OHI.

summary: You can now link each BPE code to its management, explain the stepwise course of periodontal treatment, tell scaling from root surface debridement, set up and run an ultrasonic session safely, and judge whether treatment has worked at review.

A.q: A patient is being assessed for periodontal disease. Which instrument measures periodontal pocket depths?
options: A Gracey curette for root surfaces
A.why: A graduated periodontal probe has millimetre markings, so pocket depths can be measured and recorded.

whyNot.0: A sickle scaler removes supragingival calculus.
whyNot.2: A Briault probe detects caries between teeth.
whyNot.3: A Gracey curette removes subgingival deposits; it doesn't measure.

A.q: A patient has heavy calculus and bleeding gums. What should be the initial treatment priority?
options: Refer straight away for gum surgery
OHI and removal of the deposits
A.why: The first step is oral hygiene instruction plus professional removal of plaque and calculus.

whyNot.0: Surgery is only considered for sites that don't respond to initial treatment.
whyNot.1: Antibiotics aren't a first-line treatment for gum disease.
whyNot.3: Extraction isn't the starting point; most teeth can be stabilised.

A.q: You are setting up for ultrasonic scaling. What should you check first?
options: That water flows through the tip
That the curing light is charged
A.why: Ultrasonic tips get hot and need a water coolant, so water flow is checked before use.

whyNot.1: A curing light isn't used in periodontal treatment.
whyNot.2: An amalgamator is for mixing amalgam capsules.
whyNot.3: An apex locator is for root canal treatment.

B.q: A patient returns three months after periodontal therapy. Which finding most strongly suggests improved gum health?
B.why: Reduced bleeding on probing shows inflammation has settled, the key sign that treatment has worked.

whyNot.0: Teeth can look longer as gums shrink, but that isn't the measure of success.
whyNot.2: More plaque means home care isn't working.
whyNot.3: Increasing mobility suggests disease is progressing.

B.q: During ultrasonic scaling, the patient reports sharp sensitivity. What is the best immediate response?
options: Turn up the power to finish quicker
B.why: Pausing lets the operator check the patient and adjust technique or offer local anaesthetic.

whyNot.1: More power is likely to increase discomfort.
whyNot.2: Ignoring pain is poor care and may lose the patient's trust.
whyNot.3: Switching off suction would flood the mouth with water and aerosol.

B.q: After ultrasonic work, the operator wants a hand instrument for fine residual deposits below the gum. Which is most appropriate?
B.why: Curettes have a rounded toe and back, so they can work safely below the gum on root surfaces.

whyNot.0: A sickle scaler's sharp point is designed for supragingival use and can damage the gum below the margin.
whyNot.1: A flat plastic places filling materials.
whyNot.2: A Mitchell's trimmer is a surgical and restorative instrument, not a periodontal one.

C.q: A patient has finished an initial course of gum treatment. What is the most appropriate long-term management?
options: No further care once pockets reduce
Whitening to mask the gum line
C.why: Periodontitis can return, so lifelong supportive periodontal care and good home care keep it stable.

whyNot.0: Stopping care allows the disease to return.
whyNot.1: Whitening has no effect on gum disease.

C.q: A sextant scores BPE code 4. Which action does BSP guidance recommend?
options: Oral hygiene instruction only, then recall
C.why: Code 4 (pocket over 5.5 mm) needs a full-mouth pocket chart before and after treatment, and referral should be considered.

whyNot.0: OHI alone is the management for code 1.
whyNot.3: Removing overhangs and calculus is code 2 management, not enough for code 4.

C.q: Two weeks after scaling, a patient has less bleeding but plaque persists at the gum margin. What is the best next step?
options: Repeat the full scaling at once
C.why: Persistent plaque means home care needs improving, so OHI is reinforced and tailored to the patient.

whyNot.1: Scaling can't replace daily plaque removal.
whyNot.2: Referral isn't needed just because plaque control needs improving.

reteach.title: Think of a garden path
reteach.question: Weeds grow between the paving stones of a path. A gardener can clear them, but what keeps the path clear for good?

blocks.h: The professional clears it; daily care keeps it clear
blocks.body: A professional gardener can dig out every weed and the hard roots below the surface. That's scaling and root surface debridement. But weeds come back within weeks unless someone sweeps the path every day. That's the patient's brushing and interdental cleaning, which is why OHI comes first and is reinforced at every visit. Coming back to measure the gaps between the stones is the review pocket chart. And regular visits from the gardener for life is supportive periodontal care.

explain.body: 0 nothing; 1 OHI; 2 OHI plus removing calculus and plaque traps; 3 plus root surface debridement and charting that sextant; 4 full-mouth pocket chart and consider referral. * means furcation involvement.

test.q: A sextant scores BPE code 2. What does this mean?
test.why: Code 2 means calculus or a plaque-retentive overhang, with pockets under 3.5 mm.

whyNot.1: Healthy with no bleeding is code 0.

explain.body: Scaling removes deposits above the gum. Root surface debridement removes plaque and calculus from root surfaces inside pockets, often under local anaesthetic for comfort.

explain.caption: Calculus above and below the gum: scaling reaches the first, RSD the second.

test.q: A patient with deep pockets is booked for subgingival instrumentation. Why might local anaesthetic be used?
test.why: Working deep in pockets on root surfaces can be uncomfortable, so LA keeps the patient comfortable.

whyNot.0: LA wears off within hours; it doesn't affect bleeding at home.
whyNot.3: Calculus re-forms from plaque; LA can't prevent it.

explain.body: WHO BPE probe and graduated probe for measuring. Ultrasonic scaler (water flow checked first, HVA close by). Sickle scalers above the gum; curettes below it. Over-instrumentation can lacerate the gum.

test.q: The day after periodontal instrumentation, the patient reports soreness. Which sign most suggests over-instrumentation?
test.why: Cuts or tears in the gum suggest the tissue was traumatised by over-instrumentation.

whyNot.0: Smoother surfaces are the intended result.
whyNot.1: Less bleeding is a good sign.
whyNot.2: Mild sensitivity is common after deposits are removed.

explain.body: Repeat the pocket chart and compare: less bleeding and shallower pockets mean success. Persistent plaque means reinforce OHI. Then supportive periodontal care for life.

explain.caption: Illustrative figures: a big drop in bleeding sites shows the gums are responding.

test.q: A patient asks why the pocket chart is repeated at review. What is the best explanation?
options: To compare how the tissues have responded
Because the old chart is out of date legally
test.why: Comparing the charts shows whether pockets and bleeding have reduced after treatment.

whyNot.1: Charts don't expire; they are compared over time.
whyNot.2: Whitening isn't related to pocket charting.
